summary: Lists requirements for setting up and maintaining point-to-multipoint traffic-engineered MPLS label switched paths. It deliberately avoids solution details. The requirements also cover networks beyond packet switching, such as time-division, wavelength and port switching under GMPLS. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A wish list for one sender reaching many receivers over a planned route through a network, without saying yet how to build it.

subtitle: What a signaling solution must provide to set up traffic-engineered MPLS paths that branch to many receivers.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering only supports point-to-point label switched paths, so sending one stream to many receivers means copying data at the ingress or sending duplicates through the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out requirements for signaling point-to-multipoint (P2MP) TE LSPs: one ingress, many egresses, explicit trees, adding and removing leaves, protection, re-optimization and scaling.
tldr.outcome: It specifies no protocol. Protocol solutions must satisfy these requirements and should reuse existing MPLS protocols as much as possible, applying equally to MPLS and GMPLS.

facts.label: Scaling bound
facts.value: No worse than linear in egress LSRs

today: RFC 4461 is an Informational requirements document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies no protocol, so it is a reference for what P2MP TE signaling solutions had to meet.

sections.title: Introduction, Scope and Terminology
sections.content:
MPLS traffic engineering (MPLS-TE) allows strict QoS guarantees, resource optimization and fast failure recovery, but only for point-to-point (P2P) LSPs. A P2MP TE LSP is a TE LSP that has a single ingress LSR and one or more egress LSRs, and is unidirectional. This document presents the requirements that signaling solutions for such LSPs must meet. They apply to packet-switched MPLS networks and also to L2SC, TDM, lambda and port switching networks managed by GMPLS.

The RFC says that existing mechanisms such as RFC 3209 do not support P2MP TE LSPs, so new mechanisms are needed, and that this SHOULD be achieved with maximum reuse of existing MPLS protocols.

The scope is signaling only. Out of scope are routing protocols, building the traffic engineering database, algorithms for computing trees, discovery of egress leaves, hierarchical P2MP LSPs, OAM, inter-area and inter-AS LSPs, multipoint-to-point and multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs, and application-specific requirements.

The P2MP tree is the ordered set of LSRs and TE links that make up the path from the ingress LSR to all egress LSRs. The ingress LSR starts the signaling. An egress LSR (also a leaf) is one of potentially many destinations. A branch LSR has more than one directly connected downstream LSR, and a bud LSR is an egress LSR that also has downstream LSRs attached. A P2MP-ID (P2ID) uniquely identifies the LSP and stays constant however many branches or leaves it has.

The RFC also names parts of a tree as sub-LSPs, using letters for the endpoints: S for source, L for leaf, B for branch, X for any other transit LSR, A for all and P for partial. For example, an S2L sub-LSP runs from the source to one leaf, and a B2AL sub-LSP runs from a branch to all leaves downstream of it. The S2AL sub-LSP is the whole P2MP LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the special reserved roads only go from one place to one other place. This note is about reserved roads that fork to many places, and it only talks about how to set them up, not how to plan the map.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.content:
Existing MPLS and GMPLS TE only support P2P TE LSPs. P2MP services can be built from P2P LSPs, but that is potentially suboptimal, since it may mean data replication at the ingress LSR or duplicate data traffic in the network. To serve P2MP traffic efficiently, requirements for dedicated solutions are needed.

The RFC walks through an example: a single ingress LSR serves several egress LSRs. A tree satisfying the constraints is determined in advance, and the branch LSR replicates incoming data toward its downstream neighbors. If a new receiver wants the traffic, a new tree is determined and a sub-LSP is grafted onto the existing LSP, which can turn another LSR into a branch LSR.

The RFC does not restrict the signaling protocol, but notes that the MPLS working group had chosen RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) as the signaling protocol for traffic engineering. The setup mechanism MUST be able to add and remove egress LSRs, and MUST support all TE LSP management procedures already defined for P2P TE LSPs. Computation of the tree is implementation dependent and out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: You could send the same parcel separately to each friend, but that wastes trucks. A branching route lets one truck split up only where needed, and a new friend can be added to a branch later.

sections.title: Core Requirements for Trees, Paths and Changes
sections.content:
Tree shape. The solution MUST support explicitly routed arbitrary trees, including trees where a bud LSR is both a transit and an egress node. The RFC gives two examples: a Steiner tree (cost-minimum, to save core bandwidth) and a CSPF shortest-path tree (suited to real-time traffic). Operators may use any tree computation technique. Partially specified trees via loose hops or widely scoped abstract nodes SHOULD be possible, but the egress LSRs MUST always be fully specified.

Establishment and change. Setup, maintenance and teardown MUST scale at least linearly. Solutions SHOULD support grafting to add sub-LSPs and pruning to remove them, and these operations MUST NOT disrupt traffic already flowing on the tree. Messages that are too large MUST still be handled, and the solution SHOULD NOT rely on IP fragmentation of protocol messages.

Uniform parameters. Attributes set by the ingress LSR, such as priority and bandwidth, MUST NOT vary within one P2MP LSP, giving homogeneous QoS from the root to all leaves.

Recording and resources. The solution MUST collect and update tree topology information, recording both outgoing interfaces and node-ids. It MUST support both shared and exclusive resource use, and be applicable to DiffServ-enabled networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The route must let planners choose any shape, let new leaves join or leave without interrupting everyone else, and treat every leaf the same, so nobody gets a worse connection than their neighbor.

sections.title: Failures, Re-optimization and Data Duplication
sections.content:
Failures. Detachment of leaves MUST be reported upstream, as for P2P LSPs. The solution MUST provide fast protection mechanisms similar to RFC 4090, a requirement limited to packet-switched networks. If only some egress LSRs are cut off, the ingress LSR SHOULD NOT automatically tear the whole LSP down; keeping it is a matter of local policy. A branch LSR that has lost all of its downstream leaves and cannot restore them MAY remove itself, unless it is also a bud.

Re-optimization. Make-before-break MUST be supported to minimize traffic disruption, including for a sub-tree alone, and double bandwidth reservation over shared parts must be avoided. The ingress LSR SHOULD be able to keep re-optimization source-initiated only.

Merging and duplication. A transit LSR may get several signaling messages for the same P2MP LSP. Where they refer to the same upstream interface, the result SHOULD be a single data flow. Sustained duplicate data is wasteful and can cause congestion, but it can legitimately arise during re-optimization and protection, so the solution MUST limit duplicate delivery to applications to bounded transitory conditions.

On multi-access LANs such as Ethernet, a branch LSR SHOULD be able to send one copy of the data to reach several adjacent downstream nodes, rather than one copy each.
sections.plainLanguage: If one branch of the pipe breaks, the water to the other buckets should keep flowing. When the pipes are rearranged, the new route should be built before the old one is taken apart, and nobody should get double portions for long.

sections.title: Scalability, Compatibility and GMPLS
sections.content:
Solutions MUST scale as the numbers of recipients, egress LSRs, branch LSRs and branches grow, considering refresh processing, protocol state, message counts and message size. A P2MP TE LSP with a single egress LSR should cost about as much as a P2P LSP. The RFC expects initial deployments of up to around a hundred egress LSRs, growing to several hundred within five years, and possibly more later. Scaling linearly with egress LSRs is the acceptable upper bound, and worse than linear is not acceptable. A working figure for an established LSP is less than 10% churn per day, so solutions optimize for slow change and for recovery and re-optimization rather than for fast leaf changes.

For compatibility, the solution MUST support IPv4 and IPv6, allow P2P and P2MP TE LSPs to coexist and be signaled on the same interface, and coexist with IP unicast and multicast. Legacy nodes should be usable as transit non-branch and egress LSRs where possible. LSRs should advertise capabilities such as branching support. Solutions SHOULD also support crankback so a branch LSR can reroute a sub-LSP around failures.

The mechanisms must be equally applicable to non-packet GMPLS networks and compatible with GMPLS features, though if non-packet needs over-complicate the packet solution, separate solutions may be chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The system should still work smoothly with a hundred or several hundred leaves, should not get slower than the number of leaves requires, and must not break the old one-to-one roads.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines no protocol extensions, so it changes no security model. It does require that any P2MP solution include mechanisms to enable secure establishment and management of P2MP MPLS-TE LSPs, including identifying the ingress LSR, letting signaling entities verify each other's identities, protecting control messages against spoofing and tampering, stopping unauthorized leaves or branches being added, and protecting signaling from snooping.

Solutions built on RSVP-TE are likely to inherit its security techniques and problems, which may be worse in P2MP, since an ingress LSR may need security relationships with multiple egress LSRs. The RFC compares this to IP multicast security. Solution documents MUST have detailed security sections.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the right people should be able to add a bucket or change the pipes, and nobody should be able to fake or peek at the instructions.
